title: Connection Storm: Autoscaling Makes Checkout Worse
businessContext: A retail checkout API scales from 8 to 40 pods during a flash sale. PostgreSQL has 400 connection slots, 40 of which are reserved for administration and other services. Each new pod opens a 30-connection pool.
problemStatement: Checkout p99 is 18 seconds; active client connections hit 400 and 35% of checkout requests fail. Work through three timed developments, justify your actions, and write an evidence-based incident response. The simulation starts paused; advancing time can expire unanswered decisions.
constraints: Keep database access available to on-call operators.
Do not increase max_connections or restart PostgreSQL during the sale.
Payments must retain their idempotency keys across retries.
All telemetry is synthetic. Actions only affect this practice simulation.
candidateTasks: Contain customer impact while preserving evidence and data integrity.
Respond to each new development and explain the selected action.
Cite telemetry supporting the root cause; distinguish observation from inference.
Define a permanent correction, regression coverage, recovery gates, and stakeholder update.

review.reasoning: This is a connection-budget failure rather than proof of a CPU shortage. Cap load, reserve operational access, and budget all pools together before scaling producers.

stages.title: Retry amplification arrives
stages.briefing: Payment clients retry every 200 ms. Request attempts are now five times the original arrival rate, and pool waiters outnumber executing statements.

branches.effective: The capped fleet stays within budget, but retries can undo the containment.
branches.partial: Some impact remains. Pool saturation now combines with a retry storm; extra workers cannot create database capacity.

hints: The new ceiling permits 40 x 30 = 1200 clients against 360 usable slots.
Freeze replica growth and bound checkout admission; reserve administrative access and degrade nonessential workloads.
Introduce centrally budgeted pooling or a transaction pooler after checking session-state compatibility.
alternativeApproaches: Use a validated transaction pooler to multiplex short transactions; session variables and prepared statements need compatibility testing.
Queue noninteractive checkout work with bounded depth and explicit expiration rather than keeping HTTP requests open.
commonMistakes: Scaling client pods based solely on request latency.
Increasing max_connections without accounting for memory and downstream capacity.
Blindly terminating all database sessions or retrying payments with new operation keys.
